梁越盧醜張偉梁祚平恒陳奇常爽劉獻之張吾貴劉蘭孫惠蔚徐遵明董徵刁沖盧景裕李同軌李業興
Liang Yue, Lu Chou, Zhang Wei, Liang Zuo, Ping Heng, Chen Qi, Chang Shuang, Liu Xianzhi, Zhang Wugui, Liu Lan, Sun Huiwei, Xu Zunming, Dong Zheng, Diao Chong, Lu Jingyu, Li Tonggui, and Li Yexing.
2
自晉永嘉之後，運鍾喪亂，宇內分崩，羣凶肆禍，生民不見俎豆之容，黔首唯覩戎馬之跡，禮樂文章，掃地將盡。 而契之所感，斯道猶存。 高才有德之流，自強蓬蓽； 鴻生碩儒之輩，抱器晦己。 太祖初定中原，雖日不暇給，始建都邑，便以經術為先，立太學，置五經博士生員千有餘人。 天興二年春，增國子太學生員至三千。 豈不以天下可馬上取之，不可以馬上治之，為國之道，文武兼用，毓才成務，意在茲乎？ 聖達經猷，蓋為遠矣。 四年春，命樂師入學習舞，釋菜于先聖、先師。 太宗世，改國子為中書學，立教授博士。 世祖始光三年春，別起太學於城東，後徵盧玄、高允等，而令州郡各舉才學。 於是人多砥尚，儒林轉興。 顯祖天安初，詔立鄉學，郡置博士二人，助教二人，學生六十人。 後詔：大郡立博士二人，助教四人，學生一百人； 次郡立博士二人，助教二人，學生八十人； 中郡立博士一人，助教二人，學生六十人； 下郡立博士一人，助教一人，學生四十人。 太和中，改中書學為國子學，建明堂辟雍，尊三老五更，又開皇子之學。 及遷都洛邑，詔立國子太學、四門小學。 高祖欽明稽古，篤好墳典，坐輿據鞍，不忘講道。 劉芳、李彪諸人以經書進，崔光、邢巒之徒以文史達，其餘涉獵典章，關歷詞翰，莫不縻以好爵，動貽賞眷。 於是斯文鬱然，比隆周漢。 世宗時，復詔營國學，樹小學於四門，大選儒生，以為小學博士，員四十人。 雖黌宇未立，而經術彌顯。 時天下承平，學業大盛。 故燕齊趙魏之間，橫經著錄，不可勝數。 大者千餘人，小者猶數百。 州舉茂異，郡貢孝廉，對揚王庭，每年逾眾。 神龜中，將立國學，詔以三品已上及五品清官之子以充生選。 未及簡置，仍復停寢。 正光二年，乃釋奠於國學，命祭酒崔光講孝經，始置國子生三十六人。 暨孝昌之後，海內淆亂，四方校學所存無幾。 永熙中，復釋奠於國學； 又於顯陽殿詔祭酒劉廞講孝經，黃門李郁說禮記，中書舍人盧景宣講大戴禮夏小正篇； 復置生七十二人。 及遷都於鄴，國子置生三十六人。 至於興和、武定之世，寇難既平，儒業復光矣。
After the Yongjia reign of the Jin, the times turned to ruin and chaos. The realm shattered within the four seas, villains ran rampant, and the people no longer saw ritual vessels set out—commoners saw only the hoofprints of war-horses. Ritual, music, and learning were all but swept from the earth. Yet through what moved Qi, this tradition still endured. Men of outstanding talent and virtue strengthened themselves in humble dwellings; while great scholars and eminent Confucians cherished their learning and kept themselves in obscurity. When Emperor Daowu first pacified the Central Plains, though his days left no spare moment, he founded his capital and at once made the classics his priority: he established the Imperial Academy and enrolled more than a thousand students under the Five Classics doctoral chairs. In the spring of the second year of Tianxing, enrollment at the National University and Imperial Academy was raised to three thousand. Was this not because an empire may be won from horseback but cannot be ruled from horseback—that sound governance requires both civil and military cultivation, nurturing talent to accomplish the work of state? The meaning lay precisely here. Such sagely grasp of the classics' design reached far indeed. In the spring of the fourth year he ordered music masters into the academy to learn the ritual dances and offered the vegetable sacrifice to the former sages and teachers. Under Emperor Mingyuan, the National University was renamed the Secretariat School, with instructing professors and doctoral chairs appointed. In the spring of the third year of Shiguang under Emperor Taiwu, a new Imperial Academy was built east of the city. Later Lu Xuan, Gao Yun, and others were summoned, and every prefecture and commandery was ordered to recommend men of learning and ability. Thereupon many took up the pursuit of learning, and Confucian studies revived. At the start of Tian'an under Emperor Xianwen, an edict established district schools, each commandery appointing two doctoral chairs, two teaching assistants, and sixty students. A later edict specified: large commanderies were to have two doctoral chairs, four teaching assistants, and one hundred students; secondary commanderies two doctoral chairs, two teaching assistants, and eighty students; middle commanderies one doctoral chair, two teaching assistants, and sixty students; and small commanderies one doctoral chair, one teaching assistant, and forty students. During the Taihe era the Secretariat School was restored as the National University. The Bright Hall and Imperial Academy were built, the Three Elders and Five More Venerable were honored, and instruction for imperial princes was instituted. When the court moved the capital to Luoyang, an edict established the National University, Imperial Academy, and Four Gates Elementary School. Emperor Xiaowen was reverently devoted to antiquity and deeply loved the ancient classics; whether in his carriage or on horseback, he never ceased discussing the classics. Liu Fang, Li Biao, and others rose through mastery of the classics; Cui Guang, Xing Luan, and their peers through letters and histories; and all who ranged through statutes or excelled in literary composition were rewarded with fine offices and imperial favor. Thus learning flourished abundantly, rivaling the heights of the Zhou and Han. Under Emperor Xuanwu an edict again ordered the National University rebuilt and elementary schools established at the Four Gates. A great selection of Confucian scholars was made to serve as elementary-school doctoral chairs—forty in all. Though the school buildings were not yet finished, study of the classics grew ever more prominent. The realm was at peace, and learning flourished as never before. Between Yan, Qi, Zhao, and Wei, scholars who lectured on the classics and were recorded in the rolls were beyond counting. The largest schools had more than a thousand students; even the smallest had several hundred. Prefectures recommended outstanding men, commanderies presented Filial and Incorrupt candidates, and those who appeared before the throne to expound the classics increased in number year by year. During the Shengui era, when the National University was about to be established, an edict specified that sons of third-rank officials and above and of fifth-rank pure offices should be selected as students. Before the selection could be carried out, the plan was suspended once more. In the second year of Zhengguang the libation sacrifice was held at the National University. Libationer Cui Guang was ordered to lecture on the Classic of Filial Piety, and thirty-six National University students were appointed for the first time. After the Xiaochang era the realm fell into chaos, and few schools survived anywhere in the empire. During the Yongxi era the libation sacrifice was again held at the National University; and at the Xianyang Hall Libationer Liu Yin was ordered to lecture on the Classic of Filial Piety, Huangmen Attendant Li Yu to expound the Record of Rites, and Secretariat Gentleman Lu Jingxuan to lecture on the Xiaozheng chapter of the Elder Dai's Record of Rites; seventy-two students were again enrolled. When the capital was moved to Ye, the National University enrolled thirty-six students. By the Xinghe and Wuding eras, once the wars had ended, Confucian learning flourished once more.
3
漢世鄭玄並為眾經注解，服虔、何休各有所說。 玄易、書、詩、禮、論語、孝經，虔左氏春秋，休公羊傳，大行於河北。 王肅易亦間行焉。 晉世杜預注左氏，預玄孫坦、坦弟驥於劉義隆世並為青州刺史，傳其家業，故齊地多習之。 自梁越以下傳受講說者甚眾。 今舉其知名者附列於後云。
In Han times Zheng Xuan annotated the classics comprehensively, while Fu Qian and He Xiu each had his own school of interpretation. Zheng's commentaries on the Changes, Documents, Odes, Rites, Analects, and Classic of Filial Piety, Fu's Zuo Commentary, and He's Gongyang Commentary all flourished north of the Yellow River. Wang Su's commentary on the Changes also circulated there occasionally. In Jin times Du Yu annotated the Zuo Commentary. His great-great-grandsons Tan and Ji both served as Qingzhou governors under Liu Yilong and transmitted the family tradition, so the Qi region largely followed Du Yu's school. From Liang Yue onward, those who transmitted and taught these traditions were exceedingly numerous. The well-known among them are listed below.
4
梁越，字玄覽，新興人也。 少而好學，博綜經傳，無所不通。 性純和篤信，行無擇善。 國初為禮經博士。 太祖以其謹厚，舉動可則，拜上大夫，命授諸皇子經書。 太宗即祚，以師傅之恩賜爵祝阿侯。 後出為雁門太守，獲白雀以獻，拜光祿大夫。 卒。 子弼，早卒。
Liang Yue, courtesy name Xuanlan, was a native of Xinxing. From youth he loved learning and mastered the classics and their commentaries comprehensively. His nature was pure, gentle, and deeply sincere; in conduct he never failed to do what was right. At the founding of the dynasty he served as doctoral chair in the Rites. Emperor Daowu, finding him prudent and steadfast and his conduct worthy of emulation, appointed him Grand Master and ordered him to instruct the imperial princes in the classics. When Emperor Mingyuan ascended the throne, Yue was enfeoffed as Marquis of Zhu'a in gratitude for his service as tutor. He later served as Administrator of Yanmen, presented a white sparrow he had captured, and was appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness. He died. His son Bi died young.
5
弼子恭，襲。 降為雲中子。 無子，爵除。
Bi's son Gong inherited the title. The title was reduced to Viscount of Yunzhong. He had no heir, and the title lapsed.
6
盧醜，昌黎徒河人，襄城王魯元之族也。 世祖之為監國，醜以篤學博聞入授世祖經。 後以師傅舊恩賜爵濟陰公。 除鎮軍將軍，拜尚書，加散騎常侍，出為河內太守。 延和二年冬卒。 〈闕〉 初，中山襲爵，太和中，以老疾自免。
Lu Chou was a native of Tuhe in Changli and a kinsman of Prince Lu Yuan of Xiangcheng. When Emperor Taiwu was crown prince, Chou was summoned for his devoted scholarship and broad learning to instruct the prince in the classics. Later he was enfeoffed as Duke of Jiyin in recognition of his former service as tutor. He was appointed General Who Pacifies the Army and Minister, given the additional title Regular Attendant of Scattered Cavalry, and later served as Administrator of Henei. He died in the winter of the second year of Yanhe. Text lacuna in the manuscript. Earlier, Zhongshan had inherited the title; during the Taihe era he resigned on account of age and illness.
7
子升頭，襲爵，後例降。 張偉，字仲業，小名翠螭，太原中都人也。 高祖敏，晉祕書監。 偉學通諸經，講授鄉里，受業者常數百人。 儒謹汎納，勤於教訓，雖有頑固不曉，問至數十，偉告喻殷勤，曾無慍色。 常依附經典，教以孝悌，門人感其仁化，事之如父。 性恬平，不以夷嶮易操，清雅篤慎，非法不言。 世祖時，與高允等俱被辟命，拜中書博士。 轉侍郎、大將軍樂安王範從事中郎、馮翊太守。 還，仍為中書侍郎、本國大中正。 使酒泉，慰勞沮渠無諱。 還，遷散騎侍郎。 聘劉義隆還，拜給事中、建威將軍，賜爵成臯子。 出為平東將軍、營州刺史，進爵建安公。 卒，贈征南將軍、并州刺史，諡曰康。 在州郡以仁德為先，不任刑罰，清身率下，宰守不敢為非。
His son Sheng'tou inherited the title and was later demoted by regulation. Zhang Wei, courtesy name Zhongye, childhood name Cuichi, was a native of Zhongdu in Taiyuan. His ancestor Min had been Director of the Secretariat under the Jin. Wei mastered all the classics and lectured in his home district, where his students often numbered several hundred. Confucian in bearing, prudent and broadly tolerant, he was tireless in teaching. Even when dull students failed to understand after being questioned dozens of times, Wei explained with patient care and never showed irritation. He always grounded his teaching in the classics, instructing students in filial piety and brotherly duty. His disciples, moved by his humane influence, treated him as they would a father. His nature was tranquil and even; he did not alter his conduct for prosperity or adversity. Refined and deeply prudent, he spoke only what was proper. Under Emperor Taiwu he was summoned with Gao Yun and others and appointed Doctor of the Secretariat. He was transferred to Gentleman Attendant, Attendant-in-Ordinary to Grand General Fan, Prince of Le'an, and Administrator of Fengyi. On his return he again served as Gentleman of the Secretariat and Chief Rectifier of his native commandery. He was dispatched to Jiuquan to console Juqu Wuhui. On his return he was promoted to Gentleman of Scattered Cavalry. After an embassy to Liu Yilong he was appointed Palace Attendant and General Who Establishes Might and enfeoffed as Viscount of Chenggao. He served as General Who Pacifies the East and Inspector of Yingzhou and was advanced to Duke of Jian'an. He died and was posthumously honored as General Who Conquers the South and Inspector of Bingzhou, with the posthumous name Kang. In office he put benevolence first, avoided relying on punishments, led by personal example, and local officials did not dare misconduct themselves.
8
子仲慮，太和初，假給事中、高麗副使，尋假散騎常侍、高麗使。 後出為章武太守，加寧遠將軍。
His son Zhonglü, at the start of the Taihe era, served provisionally as Palace Attendant and deputy envoy to Goguryeo, then as Regular Attendant of Scattered Cavalry and envoy to Goguryeo. He later served as Administrator of Zhangwu with the additional title General Who Pacifies the Distance.
9
仲慮弟仲繼，學尚有父風，善倉、雅、林說。 太和中，官至侍御長，坐事徙西裔，道死。
Zhonglü's younger brother Zhongji preserved his father's scholarly manner and was skilled in the Cang, Ya, and Lin commentaries. During the Taihe era he rose to Chief of Palace Attendants; convicted of an offense, he was banished to the western frontier and died on the journey.
10
梁祚，北地泥陽人。 父劭，皇始二年歸國，拜吏部郎，出為濟陽太守。 至祚居趙郡。 祚篤志好學，歷治諸經，尤善公羊春秋、鄭氏易，常以教授。 有儒者風，而無當世之才。 與幽州別駕平恒有舊，又姊先適范陽李氏，遂攜家人僑居於薊。 積十餘年，雖覊旅貧窘而著述不倦。 恒時相請屈，與論經史。 辟祕書中散，稍遷祕書令。 為李訢所排，擯退為中書博士。 後出為統萬鎮司馬，徵為散令。 撰并陳壽三國志，名曰國統。 又作代都賦，頗行於世。 清貧守素，不交勢貴。 年八十七，太和十二年卒。
Liang Zuo was a native of Niyang in Beidi. His father Shao submitted to the Wei in the second year of Huangshi, was appointed Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel, and later served as Administrator of Jiyang. By Zuo's time the family had settled in Zhao commandery. Zuo was devoted to learning, studied all the classics in turn, and was especially skilled in the Gongyang Commentary and Zheng Xuan's Changes, which he taught throughout his life. He had the bearing of a Confucian scholar but lacked talent for practical affairs of his time. He was an old friend of Ping Heng, Vice-Prefect of Youzhou, and his elder sister had earlier married into the Li clan of Fanyang; he therefore moved his family to live as sojourners in Ji. For more than ten years, though living abroad in poverty, he never wearied of writing. Ping Heng often invited him to visit and discuss the classics and histories. He was summoned as Secretariat Attendant and gradually promoted to Secretariat Director. Ostracized by Li Xin, he was demoted to Doctor of the Secretariat. He later served as Military Administrator of the Tongwan garrison and was recalled as Scattered Cavalry Commandant. He compiled a unified edition of Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms, entitled National Succession. He also wrote the Rhapsody on the Capital of Dai, which circulated widely in his day. Poor but upright, he kept to simplicity and did not associate with the powerful. He died in the twelfth year of Taihe at the age of eighty-seven.
11
子元吉，有父風。
His son Yuanji preserved his father's scholarly manner.
12
少子重，歷碎職，後為相州鎮北府參軍事。
His youngest son Chong held various minor posts and later served as Military Adjutant of the Northern Garrison Headquarters of Xiangzhou.
13
平恒，字繼叔，燕國薊人。 祖視，父儒，並仕慕容為通宦。 恒耽勤讀誦，研綜經籍，鉤深致遠，多所博聞。 自周以降，暨於魏世，帝王傳代之由，貴臣昇降之緒，皆撰錄品第，商略是非，號曰略注，合百餘篇。 好事者覽之，咸以為善焉。 安貧樂道，不以屢空改操。 徵為中書博士。 久之，出為幽州別駕。 廉貞寡欲，不營資產，衣食至常不足，妻子不免飢寒。 後拜著作佐郎，遷祕書丞。
Ping Heng, courtesy name Jishu, was a native of Ji in Yan. His grandfather Shi and father Ru both served the Murong as general officials. Heng devoted himself to reading and recitation, mastered the classics comprehensively, plumbed profound depths, and acquired broad learning. From the Zhou through the Wei, he compiled and ranked the reasons for dynastic succession and the rises and falls of eminent ministers, weighing right and wrong in a work entitled Brief Notes of more than a hundred chapters. Readers who delighted in such matters all praised it highly. Content with poverty and devoted to the Way, he never altered his conduct despite repeated want. He was summoned as Doctor of the Secretariat. After some time he served as Vice-Prefect of Youzhou. Pure and upright with few desires, he pursued no wealth; his food and clothing were often insufficient, and his wife and children knew hunger and cold. He was later appointed Assistant Gentleman of Composition and promoted to Secretariat Assistant Director.
14
時高允為監，河間邢祐、[2]北平陽嘏、河東裴定、廣平程駿、金城趙元順等為著作佐郎，雖才學互有短長，然俱為稱職，並號長者。 允每稱博通經籍無過恒也。
At the time Gao Yun served as supervisor, with Xing You of Hejian, [2] Yang Gu of Beiping, Pei Ding of Hedong, Cheng Jun of Guangping, Zhao Yuanshun of Jincheng, and others as Assistant Gentlemen of Composition. Though their talents varied, all performed their duties well and were known as the elders. Gao Yun often said that no one surpassed Heng in mastery of the classics.
15
恒即劉彧將軍王玄謨舅子。 恒三子，並不率父業，好酒自棄。 恒常忿其世衰，植杖巡舍側崗而哭，不為營事婚宦，任意官娶，故仕聘濁碎，不得及其門流。 恒婦弟鄧宗慶及外生孫玄明等每以為言。 恒曰：「此輩會是衰頓，何煩勞我。 」乃別構精廬，并置經籍於其中，一奴自給，妻子莫得而往，酒食亦不與同。 時有珍美，呼時老東安公刁雍等共飲噉之，家人無得嘗焉。 太和十年，以恒為祕書令，而恒固請為郡，未授而卒，時年七十六。 贈平東將軍、幽州刺史、都昌侯，諡曰康。
Heng was the nephew by marriage of Liu Yu's general Wang Xuemo. Heng's three sons all failed to follow their father's example, loving wine and ruining themselves. Heng often grieved at his family's decline, leaning on his staff to weep on the hill beside his house. He arranged no marriages or offices for his sons, letting them marry as they pleased; their matches were unworthy and could not sustain the family's standing. His wife's younger brother Deng Zongqing and his sister's son Sun Xuanming often urged him about this. Heng said, "These fellows are bound to decline—why should they trouble me?" He then built a separate study lodge, stocked it with classics, and kept only one servant; his wife and children were not permitted to enter, nor did he share meals with them. When delicacies were available he summoned the venerable Duke of Dong'an, Diao Yong, and others to share them; his family tasted none. In the tenth year of Taihe he was appointed Secretariat Director, but firmly requested a commandery post; before the appointment was made he died at seventy-six. He was posthumously honored as General Who Pacifies the East, Inspector of Youzhou, and Marquis of Duchang, with the posthumous name Kang.
16
子壽昌，太和初，祕書令史。 稍遷荊州征虜府錄事參軍。
His son Shouchang served as Secretariat Clerk at the start of the Taihe era. He was later promoted to Recording Secretary of the Pacification Headquarters of Jingzhou.
17
陳奇，字脩奇，河北人也，自云晉涼州刺史驤之八世孫。 祖刃，仕慕容垂。 奇少孤，家貧，而奉母至孝。 齠齓聰識，有夙成之美。 性氣剛亮，與俗不羣。 愛玩經典，博通墳籍，常非馬融、鄭玄解經失旨，志在著述五經。 始注孝經、論語，頗傳於世，為搢紳所稱。
Chen Qi, courtesy name Xiuqi, was a native of Hebei who claimed descent in the eighth generation from Xiang, Jin Inspector of Liangzhou. His grandfather Ren served Murong Chui. Orphaned young and poor, Qi nevertheless served his mother with utmost filial devotion. Even in childhood he was clever and perceptive, showing precocious brilliance. His nature was firm and forthright; he kept apart from common society. He loved the classics and mastered the ancient texts, often criticizing Ma Rong and Zheng Xuan for misinterpreting them, and aspired to write commentaries on the Five Classics. He first annotated the Classic of Filial Piety and the Analects, which circulated widely and won praise from the gentry.
18
與河間邢祐同召赴京。 時祕書監游雅素聞其名，始頗好之，引入祕省，欲授以史職。 後與奇論典誥及詩書，雅贊扶馬鄭。 至於易訟卦天與水違行，雅曰：「自葱嶺以西，水皆西流，推此而言，易之所及自葱嶺以東耳。 」奇曰：「易理綿廣，包含宇宙。 若如公言，自葱嶺以西，豈東向望天哉？ 」奇執義非雅，每如此類，終不苟從。 雅性護短，因以為嫌。 嘗眾辱奇，或爾汝之，或指為小人。 奇曰：「公身為君子，奇身且小人耳。 」雅曰：「君言身且小人，君祖父是何人也？ 」奇曰：「祖，燕東部侯釐。 」[3]雅質奇曰：「侯釐何官也？ 」奇曰：「三皇不傳禮，官名豈同哉？ 故昔有雲師、火正、鳥師之名。 以斯而言，世革則官異，時易則禮變。 公為皇魏東宮內侍長，侍長竟何職也？ 」由是雅深憾之。 先是敕以奇付雅，令銓補祕書，雅既惡之，遂不復敍用焉。
He was summoned to the capital together with Xing You of Hejian. Secretariat Director You Ya had long heard of his reputation, initially favored him, brought him into the Secretariat, and wished to assign him historical duties. Later, debating with Qi on the canonical edicts and the Odes and Documents, Ya upheld Ma Rong and Zheng Xuan. On the Song hexagram—Heaven and Water moving contrary to each other—Ya said, "West of the Cong Mountains all rivers flow westward; by this reasoning, the Changes applies only east of the Cong Mountains." Qi replied, "The principles of the Changes are vast and embrace the entire cosmos." If that were so, would people west of the Cong Mountains not still face east to behold Heaven?" Qi held to principle against Ya; on such matters he never yielded casually. Ya was defensive of his own faults and therefore came to resent him. He once humiliated Qi in public, addressing him familiarly or calling him a petty man. Qi replied, "You are a gentleman; I am merely a petty man." Ya said, "You call yourself a petty man—what sort of men were your grandfather and father?" Qi replied, "My grandfather was Xi, Marquis of the Eastern Division of Yan." [3] Ya pressed him: "What office did Marquis Xi hold?" Qi replied, "The Three Sovereigns did not transmit ritual—how could office titles remain the same?" Hence antiquity knew titles such as Cloud Master, Fire Rectifier, and Bird Master. By this reasoning, when ages change offices differ, and when times shift ritual transforms. You served as Chief Palace Attendant of the Eastern Palace of Great Wei—what office is that, after all?" From this Ya bore deep resentment toward him. An earlier edict had placed Qi under Ya to assess him for Secretariat appointment; since Ya detested him, he never arranged his appointment.
19
奇冗散數年，高允與奇讎溫古籍，嘉其遠致，稱奇通識，非凡學所窺。 允微勸雅曰：「君朝望具瞻，何為與野儒辨簡牘章句？ 」雅謂允有私於奇，曰：「君寧黨小人也！ 」乃取奇所注論語、孝經焚於坑內。 奇曰：「公貴人，不乏樵薪，何乃燃奇論語？ 」雅愈怒，因告京師後生不聽傳授。 而奇無降志，亦評雅之失。 雅製昭皇太后碑文，論后名字之美，比諭前魏之甄后。 奇刺發其非，遂聞於上。 詔下司徒檢對碑史事，乃郭后，雅有屈焉。
Qi remained idle for several years. Gao Yun studied ancient texts with him, praised his far-reaching insight, and declared his learning beyond ordinary scholarship. Gao Yun gently urged Ya, "Your prestige at court is universally watched—why debate textual minutiae with a rustic scholar?" Ya thought Yun favored Qi and said, "Are you not siding with a petty man!" He then took Qi's annotated Analects and Classic of Filial Piety and burned them in a pit. Qi said, "You are a nobleman with no lack of firewood—why burn my Analects?" Ya grew angrier still and forbade the young scholars of the capital to study under him. Yet Qi did not lower his resolve and continued to criticize Ya's faults. Ya composed the epitaph for Empress Dowager Zhao, praising the beauty of her name and comparing her to Empress Zhen of Former Wei. Qi exposed the error, and the matter reached the throne. An edict ordered the Minister of Works to verify the historical facts; the empress was in fact Empress Guo, and Ya was proven wrong.
20
有人為謗書，多怨時之言，頗稱奇不得志。 雅乃諷在事云：「此書言奇不遂，當是奇假人為之。 如依律文，造謗書者皆及孥戮。 」遂抵奇罪。 時司徒、平原王陸麗知奇見枉，惜其才學，故得遷延經年，冀有寬宥。 但執以獄成，竟致大戮，遂及其家。 奇於易尤長，在獄嘗自筮卦，未及成，乃擥破而歎曰：「吾不度來年冬季！ 」及奇受害，如其所占。
Someone composed a slanderous book full of complaints against the times that spoke of Qi's frustrated ambitions. Ya then insinuated to officials, "This book speaks of Qi's failure—Qi must have had someone write it for him." Under the law, those who compose slanderous books are punished together with their families. Charges were then laid against Qi. The Minister of Works, Prince of Pingyuan Lu Li, knew Qi was wronged and valued his talent, delaying the case for years in hope of pardon. But once the case was concluded in prison, he was executed and his family implicated as well. Qi was especially skilled in the Changes; in prison he once divined for himself, but before completing the hexagram he broke the stalks and sighed, "I do not expect to survive the coming winter!" When Qi was executed, events unfolded exactly as he had divined.
21
奇初被召，夜夢星墜壓脚，明而告人曰：「星則好風，星則好雨，夢星壓脚，必無善徵。 但時命峻切，不敢不赴耳。 」奇妹適常氏，有子曰矯之，仕歷郡守。 神龜中，上書陳時政所宜，言頗忠至，清河王懌稱美之。 奇所注論語，矯之傳掌，未能行於世，其義多異鄭玄，往往與司徒崔浩同。
When Qi was first summoned, he dreamed that a star fell upon his foot. At dawn he told others, "Stars presage wind and rain—a star falling on one's foot can hardly be auspicious." But the summons was urgent—I dared not refuse." Qi's younger sister married into the Chang clan; her son Jiaozhi rose to serve as commandery administrator. During the Shengui era he submitted a memorial on current policy that was notably loyal and sincere; Prince of Qinghe Yuan Yi praised it. Qi's annotated Analects was preserved by Jiaozhi but never circulated widely; its interpretations often differed from Zheng Xuan and frequently agreed with Minister of Works Cui Hao.
22
常爽，字仕明，河內溫人，魏太常卿林六世孫也。 祖珍，苻堅南安太守，因世亂遂居涼州。 父坦，乞伏世鎮遠將軍、大夏鎮將、顯美侯。 爽少而聰敏，嚴正有志概，雖家人僮隸未嘗見其寬誕之容。 篤志好學，博聞強識，明習緯候，五經百家多所研綜。 州郡禮命皆不就。
Chang Shuang, courtesy name Shiming, was a native of Wen in Henei and sixth-generation descendant of Lin, Wei Grand Master of Ceremonies. His grandfather Zhen served as Administrator of Nan'an under Fu Jian and settled in Liangzhou during the turmoil of the age. His father Tan served the Qifu as General Who Pacifies the Distance, Garrison Commander of Daxia, and Marquis of Xianmei. From youth Shuang was clever and keen, stern and upright; even family servants never saw him with a lax or unrestrained manner. Devoted to learning, broadly informed with a strong memory, versed in prognostic texts, he mastered the Five Classics and the hundred schools. He declined all courteous summons from prefectures and commanderies.
23
世祖西征涼土，爽與兄仕國歸款軍門，世祖嘉之。 賜仕國爵五品，顯美男； 爽為六品，拜宣威將軍。 是時戎車屢駕，征伐為事，貴遊子弟未遑學術，爽置館溫水之右，教授門徒七百餘人，京師學業，翕然復興。 爽立訓甚有勸罰之科，弟子事之若嚴君焉。 尚書左僕射元贊、平原太守司馬真安、著作郎程靈虬，皆是爽教所就。 崔浩、高允並稱爽之嚴教，奬厲有方。 允曰：「文翁柔勝，先生剛克，立教雖殊，成人一也。 」其為通識歎服如此。
When Emperor Taiwu campaigned west against Liang, Shuang and his elder brother Shiguo submitted at the army gate, and the emperor commended them. Shiguo was enfeoffed as fifth-rank Baron of Xiannan; Shuang received sixth rank and was appointed General Who Proclaims Might. War chariots were constantly deployed and campaigns the order of the day; sons of the nobility had no leisure for study. Shuang established a school on the right bank of the Wen River and instructed more than seven hundred disciples, and learning in the capital flourished anew. Shuang established strict rules of reward and punishment; his disciples served him as they would a stern master. Left Vice Minister Yuan Zan, Administrator of Pingyuan Sima Zhen'an, and Gentleman of Composition Cheng Lingqiu were all products of Shuang's teaching. Cui Hao and Gao Yun both praised Shuang's stern instruction and well-directed encouragement. Gao Yun said, "Wen Weng overcame through gentleness; the Master through firmness—though their methods differed, both shaped worthy men." Such was the comprehensive understanding with which men admired him.
24
因教授之暇，述六經略注，以廣制作，甚有條貫。 其序曰：「傳稱：『立天之道曰陰與陽，立地之道曰柔與剛，立人之道曰仁與義。 』然則仁義者人之性也，經典者身之文也，皆以陶鑄神情，啟悟耳目，未有不由學而能成其器，不由習而能利其業。 是故季路勇士也，服道以成忠烈之概； 甯越庸夫也，講藝以全高尚之節。 蓋所由者習也，所因者本也，本立而道生，身文而德備焉。 昔者先王之訓天下也，莫不導以詩書，教以禮樂，移其風俗，和其人民。 故恭儉莊敬而不煩者，教深於禮也； 廣博易良而不奢者，教深於樂也； 溫柔敦厚而不愚者，教深於詩也； 疏通知遠而不誣者，教深於書也； 潔靜精微而不賊者，教深於易也； 屬辭比事而不亂者，教深於春秋也。 夫樂以和神，詩以正言，禮以明體，書以廣聽，春秋以斷事，五者蓋五常之道相須而備，而易為之源。 故曰：「易不可見則乾坤其幾乎息矣。 」由是言之，六經者先王之遺烈，聖人之盛事也。 安可不遊心寓目，習性文身哉！ 頃因暇日，屬意藝林，略撰所聞，討論其本，名曰六經略注以訓門徒焉。 」其略注行於世。
In intervals between teaching he composed Brief Commentaries on the Six Classics to extend the canonical tradition, arranged with excellent systematic order. Its preface reads: "The tradition states: 'Establishing Heaven's Way means yin and yang; establishing Earth's Way means soft and hard; establishing Man's Way means benevolence and righteousness.'" Thus benevolence and righteousness are human nature, and the classics are the ornament of the person—both mold spirit and enlighten the mind. No one has ever perfected his character without learning, or mastered his craft without practice. Thus Zilu was a brave warrior, yet by submitting to the Way he achieved loyal valor; Ning Yue was a common fellow, yet by studying the arts he preserved exalted integrity. What one follows is practice; what one relies on is the root. When the root is established the Way arises; when the person is cultivated, virtue is complete. Of old the former kings instructed the realm by guiding it with the Odes and Documents, teaching it with ritual and music, transforming its customs, and harmonizing its people. Thus those who are reverent, frugal, dignified, and respectful without vexation have been deeply taught by ritual; those who are broad-minded, easy, and good without extravagance have been deeply taught by music; those who are gentle, soft, and sincere without foolishness have been deeply taught by the Odes; those who are penetrating, intelligent, and far-seeing without deception have been deeply taught by the Documents; those who are pure, tranquil, subtle, and refined without harm have been deeply taught by the Changes; those who arrange words and compare events without disorder have been deeply taught by the Spring and Autumn. Music harmonizes the spirit; the Odes rectify speech; ritual clarifies form; the Documents broaden understanding; the Spring and Autumn adjudicate affairs. These five embody the Way of the five constants, mutually sustaining one another—and the Changes are their source. Thus it is said: "If the Changes cannot be seen, Heaven and Earth would almost come to rest." From this it follows that the Six Classics are the enduring legacy of the former kings and the supreme accomplishment of the sages. How could one fail to give one's heart and attention to them, cultivate one's nature, and adorn one's person through them! Recently, on a day of leisure, I turned my attention to the forest of learning, briefly set down what I have heard, examined their foundations, and named the work Brief Commentaries on the Six Classics to instruct my disciples. His Brief Commentaries circulated in the world.
25
爽不事王侯，獨守閑靜，講肄經典二十餘年，時人號為「儒林先生」。 年六十三，卒於家。
Shuang did not serve kings or marquises. He lived alone in quiet seclusion, lecturing and studying the classics for more than twenty years, and men of the age called him "Master Lin of the Confucians." He died at home at the age of sixty-three.
26
子文通，歷官至鎮西司馬、南天水太守、西翼校尉。 文通子景，別有傳。
His son Wentong rose through the ranks to serve as General Who Pacifies the West, Administrator of Southern Tianshui, and Colonel of the Western Wing. Wentong's son Jing has a separate biography.
27
劉獻之，博陵饒陽人也。 少而孤貧，雅好詩、傳，曾受業於勃海程玄，後遂博觀眾籍。 見名法之言，掩卷而笑曰：「若使楊墨之流不為此書，千載誰知其小也！ 」曾謂其所親曰：「觀屈原離騷之作，自是狂人，死其宜矣，何足惜也！ 吾常謂濯纓洗耳，有異人之迹； 哺糟歠醨，有同物之志。 而孔子曰：『我則異於是，無可無不可。 』誠哉斯言，實獲我心。」
Liu Xianzhi was a native of Raoyang in Boling. Orphaned and poor from youth, he naturally loved the Odes and the Commentary. He once studied under Cheng Xuan of Bohai and afterward read widely among many texts. When he encountered Legalist writings, he would close the scroll and laugh, saying, "If Yang Zhu, Mozi, and their followers had not written this book, who after a thousand years would know how small-minded they were!" Once he told those close to him, "Reading Qu Yuan's Li Sao, one sees plainly a madman. His death was fitting—what is there to regret!" I often say that washing one's cap-strings and washing one's ears show the marks of extraordinary men; while sucking lees and drinking dregs shows the mind of one who has become one with what he consumes. Yet Confucius said, 'I for my part am not like this—there is nothing I insist on, and nothing I insist against.' Truly that saying—it speaks directly to my heart."
28
時人有從獻之學者，獻之輒謂之曰：「人之立身，雖百行殊途，準之四科，要以德行為首。 君若能入孝出悌，忠信仁讓，不待出戶，天下自知。 儻不能然，雖復下帷針股，躡屩從師，正可博聞多識，不過為土龍乞雨，眩惑將來，其於立身之道有何益乎？ 孔門之徒，初亦未悟，見臯魚之歎，方歸而養親。 [4]嗟乎先達，何自覺之晚也！ 束脩不易，受之亦難，敢布心腹，子其圖之。 」由是四方學者莫不高其行義而希造其門。
When men came to study under Xianzhi, he always told them, "In establishing oneself, though the hundred practices follow different paths, measured by the four categories of disciples, conduct and virtue must come first. If you can be filial at home and respectful abroad, loyal, trustworthy, benevolent, and forbearing, the world will know of you without your ever leaving your door. If you cannot be thus, even if you study behind closed curtains, pin your thigh to stay awake, and wear straw sandals to follow a teacher, you may become broadly informed at best—nothing more than a clay dragon used to pray for rain, dazzling future generations. What good is that for the art of living? Even disciples of Confucius's school at first failed to understand; only after hearing Gaoyu's lament did they return home to care for their parents. [4] Alas, you who have gone before—why do you awaken to this only so late! The ceremonial gift of dried meat is not lightly given, nor is instruction easily received. I dare lay bare my inmost thoughts—consider this carefully. From this, scholars from all directions admired his conduct and righteousness and hoped to study at his gate.
29
獻之善春秋、毛詩，每講左氏，盡隱公八年便止，云義例已了，不復須解。 由是弟子不能究竟其說。 後本郡舉孝廉，非其好也，逼遣之，乃應命，至京，稱疾而還。 高祖幸中山，詔徵典內校書，獻之喟然歎曰：「吾不如莊周散木遠矣！ 一之謂甚，其可再乎。 」固以疾辭。 時中山張吾貴與獻之齊名，海內皆曰儒宗。 吾貴每一講唱，門徒千數，其行業可稱者寡。 獻之著錄，數百而已，皆經通之士。 於是有識者辨其優劣。 魏承喪亂之後，五經大義雖有師說，而海內諸生多有疑滯，咸決於獻之。 六藝之文，雖不悉注，然所標宗旨，頗異舊義，撰三禮大義四卷，三傳略例三卷，注毛詩序義一卷，今行於世，并章句疏三卷。 注湼槃經未就而卒。 有四子，放古、爰古、參古、脩古。
Xianzhi excelled in the Spring and Autumn and the Mao Odes. Each time he lectured on the Zuo Commentary he stopped at the eighth year of Duke Yin, saying the principles and patterns were complete and needed no further explanation. Because of this his disciples could never fully master his teaching. Later his home commandery recommended him as Filial and Incorrupt. It was not to his liking, but he was compelled to go. He accepted the summons, reached the capital, pleaded illness, and returned home. When Emperor Xiaowen visited Zhongshan, an edict summoned him to direct the collation of books within the palace. Xianzhi sighed deeply and said, "I am far from matching Zhuang Zhou's useless tree! Once is already too much—how could it happen again? He firmly declined on grounds of illness. At the time Zhang Wugui of Zhongshan was equally renowned with Xianzhi; throughout the empire both were hailed as patriarchs of Confucian learning. Each time Wugui lectured his disciples numbered in the thousands, yet few among them had conduct or achievement worth praising. Xianzhi's registered disciples numbered only in the hundreds, yet all were scholars who had thoroughly mastered the classics. Thereupon men of discernment judged which of the two was superior. Wei inherited the aftermath of war and disorder. Though the great meaning of the Five Classics had masters' explanations, many students throughout the empire still harbored doubts—and all resolved them through Xianzhi. Though he did not annotate all the texts of the Six Arts, the principles he set forth differed considerably from older interpretations. He compiled Great Meanings of the Three Rites in four juan, Brief Patterns of the Three Commentaries in three juan, and Annotation on the Meaning of the Preface to the Mao Odes in one juan—all still in circulation—together with Commentary and Sentence Glosses in three juan. He was annotating the Nirvana Sutra but died before finishing the work. He had four sons: Fanggu, Yuangu, Cangu, and Xiugu.
30
放古，幼有人才。 為州從事，早亡。
Fanggu showed talent from youth. He served as a commandery aide and died young.
31
爰古、參古，並傳父詩而不能精通也。
Yuangu and Cangu both inherited their father's Odes but could not master them fully.
32
張吾貴，字吳子，中山人。 少聰惠口辯，身長八尺，容貌奇偉。 年十八，本郡舉為太學博士。 吾貴先未多學，乃從酈詮受禮，牛天祐受易。 詮、祐粗為開發，而吾貴覽讀一遍，便即別構戶牖。 世人競歸之。 曾在夏學，聚徒千數而不講傳，生徒竊云張生之於左氏似不能說。 吾貴聞之，謂其徒曰：「我今夏講暫罷，後當說傳，君等來日皆當持本。 」生徒怪之而已。 吾貴謂劉蘭云：「君曾讀左氏，為我一說。 」蘭遂為講。 三旬之中，吾貴兼讀杜、服，隱括兩家，異同悉舉。 諸生後集，便為講之，義例無窮，皆多新異。 蘭乃伏聽。 學者以此益奇之。 而以辯能飾非，好為詭說，由是業不久傳，而氣陵牧守，不屈王侯，竟不仕而終。
Zhang Wugui, courtesy name Wuzi, was a native of Zhongshan. From youth he was clever and eloquent, eight feet tall, with a striking and imposing appearance. At eighteen his home commandery recommended him as doctoral chair of the Imperial University. Wugui had not studied much at first. He then studied Rites under Li Quan and the Changes under Niu Tianyou. Quan and You gave him only a rough introduction, yet Wugui read each text through once and at once developed his own independent interpretations. Scholars everywhere flocked to him. He once taught at a summer academy, gathering more than a thousand disciples without ever lecturing on the Commentary. Students whispered among themselves that Master Zhang seemed unable to expound the Zuo Commentary. Wugui heard this and told his disciples, "My summer lectures are temporarily suspended. Later I will expound the Commentary—you must all bring your texts on the appointed day." The students found it strange, that was all. Wugui said to Liu Lan, "You have read the Zuo Commentary—lecture on it for me." Lan then lectured. Within thirty days Wugui read both Du Yu and Fu Qian in full, synthesized the two schools, and set forth all their points of agreement and disagreement. When the students gathered afterward, he lectured at once—principles and patterns without end, nearly all of them novel and unusual. Lan listened humbly from below. Scholars admired him all the more for this. Yet because he used debate to cover his errors and loved to spin clever sophistries, his learning did not long endure. Overbearing toward prefects and governors, he bowed to neither kings nor marquises, never took office, and died in that state.
33
劉蘭，武邑人。 年三十餘，始入小學，書急就篇。 家人覺其聰敏，遂令從師，受春秋、詩、禮於中山王保安。 家貧無以自資，且耕且學。 三年之後，便白其兄：「蘭欲講書。 」其兄笑而聽之，為立黌舍，聚徒二百。 蘭讀左氏，五日一遍，兼通五經。 先是張吾貴以聰辨過人，其所解說，不本先儒之旨。 唯蘭推經、傳之由，本注者之意，參以緯候及先儒舊事，甚為精悉。 自後經義審博，皆由於蘭。 蘭又明陰陽，博物多識，為儒者所宗。 瀛州刺史裴植徵蘭講書於州城南館，植為學主，故生徒甚盛，海內稱焉。 又特為中山王英所重。 英引在館，令授其子熙、誘、略等。 蘭學徒前後數千，成業者眾，而排毀公羊，又非董仲舒，由是見譏於世。 永平中，為國子助教。 延昌中，靜坐讀書，有人叩門，門人通焉，蘭命引入。 其人葛巾單衣，入與蘭坐，謂蘭曰：「君自是學士，何為每見毀辱，理義長短，竟知在誰，而過無禮見陵也。 今欲相召，當與君正之。 」言終而出。 出後，蘭告家人。 少時而患卒。
Liu Lan was a native of Wuyi. Not until he was over thirty did he enter elementary school and copy out the Rapid Primer. His family saw how clever he was and had him study under a teacher, learning the Spring and Autumn, Odes, and Rites from Wang Bao'an of Zhongshan. His family was too poor to support him, so he farmed and studied at the same time. After three years he told his elder brother, "Lan wishes to lecture on the classics." His elder brother laughed but agreed, built a school hall, and gathered two hundred disciples. Lan read through the Zuo Commentary once every five days and mastered all Five Classics. Previously Zhang Wugui's brilliance and eloquence surpassed others, but his explications did not rest on the intent of earlier Confucians. Only Lan traced the origins of the classics and commentaries, grounded his work in the annotators' intent, and consulted prognostic texts and old accounts of earlier Confucians—making his scholarship exceedingly precise and thorough. From then on, the depth and breadth of classical interpretation owed everything to Lan. Lan was also versed in yin and yang, broadly learned and deeply knowledgeable, and was revered by Confucian scholars. Pei Zhi, Inspector of Yingzhou, summoned Lan to lecture at the south hall of the prefecture. Zhi served as master of the school, and disciples were exceedingly numerous—Lan was famed throughout the empire. He was also especially valued by Prince of Zhongshan Yuan Ying. Ying brought him into his residence and had him instruct his sons Xi, You, Lue, and the others. Lan's disciples over the years numbered in the thousands and many completed their training, yet because he rejected and denounced the Gongyang Commentary and also criticized Dong Zhongshu, he was mocked by the world. During the Yongping era he served as Assistant Instructor of the National University. During the Yanqu era he was reading quietly when someone knocked at the door. A disciple announced the visitor, and Lan ordered him admitted. The man wore a hemp headcloth and simple clothes. Entering, he sat with Lan and said, "You are a scholar—why do you suffer insult after insult? Whether doctrine and principle are right or wrong, who can ultimately say? Yet you are overcome rudely and without courtesy. Now I wish to summon you—we shall settle this with you." Having finished speaking, he went out. After the visitor left, Lan told his family what had happened. Shortly afterward he was stricken and died suddenly.
34
孫惠蔚，字叔炳，武邑武遂人也，小字陀羅。 自言六世祖道恭為晉長秋卿，自道恭至惠蔚世以儒學相傳。 惠蔚年十三，粗通詩、書及孝經、論語； 十八，師董道季講易； 十九，師程玄讀禮經及春秋三傳。 周流儒肆，有名於冀方。
Sun Huiwei, courtesy name Shubing, was a native of Wusui in Wuyi; his childhood name was Tuoluo. He said his sixth-generation ancestor Dao Gong had been Jin Director of the Palace Parks, and from Dao Gong down to Huiwei the family had transmitted Confucian learning from generation to generation. At thirteen Huiwei had a rough mastery of the Odes, Documents, Classic of Filial Piety, and Analects; at eighteen he studied the Changes under Dong Daoji; at nineteen he studied under Cheng Xuan, reading the Classic of Rites and the three commentaries on the Spring and Autumn. He traveled among Confucian schools and was renowned throughout the Ji region.
35
太和初，郡舉孝廉，對策於中書省。 時中書監高閭宿聞惠蔚，稱其英辯，因相談，薦為中書博士。 轉皇宗博士。 閭被敕理定雅樂，惠蔚參其事。 及樂成，閭上疏請集朝貴於太樂，共研是非。 祕書令李彪自以才辯，立難於其間，閭命惠蔚與彪抗論，彪不能屈。 黃門侍郎張彝常與遊處，每表疏論事，多參訪焉。 十七年，高祖南征，上議告類之禮。 及太師馮熙薨，惠蔚監其喪禮，上書令熙未冠之子皆服成人之服。 惠蔚與李彪以儒學相知，及彪位至尚書，惠蔚仍太廟令。 高祖曾從容言曰：「道固既登龍門而孫蔚猶沉涓澮，朕常以為負矣。 」雖久滯小官，深體通塞，無孜孜之望，儒者以是尚焉。
At the beginning of the Taihe era his commandery recommended him as Filial and Incorrupt, and he answered imperial questions at the Secretariat. At that time Secretariat Supervisor Gao Lu had long heard of Huiwei and praised his eloquent brilliance. After conversing with him, Lu recommended him as Secretariat doctoral chair. He was transferred to the post of Imperial Clan doctoral chair. Lu received orders to arrange and fix the court music, and Huiwei participated in the work. When the music was complete, Lu submitted a memorial requesting that court nobles be gathered at the Grand Music Office to debate its merits together. Secretariat Director Li Biao, confident in his talent and eloquence, raised objections in their midst. Lu ordered Huiwei to debate him, and Biao could not prevail. Yellow Gate Attendant Zhang Yi often kept company with him and frequently consulted him when drafting memorials on state affairs. In the seventeenth year Emperor Xiaowen campaigned south, and the court debated the rites of announcing victory to Heaven and Earth. When Grand Preceptor Feng Xi died, Huiwei oversaw the mourning rites and submitted a memorial that Xi's sons who had not yet come of age should wear adult mourning garments. Huiwei and Li Biao had become friends through their shared Confucian learning. When Biao rose to Minister of the Secretariat, Huiwei remained Director of the Imperial Ancestral Temple. Emperor Xiaowen once remarked at leisure, "Daogu has already passed through the Dragon Gate while Sun Wei still lingers in a shallow ditch—I have always felt I owed him better." Though long confined to minor office, he deeply understood the alternation of obstruction and success and harbored no restless ambition—Confucian scholars held him in esteem for this.
36
二十二年，侍讀東宮。 先是七廟以平文為太祖，高祖議定祖宗，以道武為太祖。 祖宗雖定，然昭穆未改。 及高祖崩，祔神主於廟，時侍中崔光兼太常卿，以太祖既改，昭穆以次而易。 兼御史中尉、黃門侍郎邢巒以為太祖雖改，昭穆仍不應易，乃立彈草欲按奏光。 光謂惠蔚曰：「此乃禮也，而執法欲見彈劾，思獲助於碩學。 」惠蔚曰：「此深得禮變。 」尋為書以與光，讚明其事。 光以惠蔚書呈宰輔，乃召惠蔚與巒庭議得失，尚書令王肅又助巒，而巒理終屈，彈事遂寢。
In the twenty-second year he served as reader attendant in the Eastern Palace. Previously the seven ancestral temples had taken Emperor Pingwen as High Ancestor. Emperor Xiaowen deliberated on fixing the imperial ancestors and made Emperor Daowu the High Ancestor. Although the imperial ancestors had been fixed, the zhao-mu temple order had not yet been adjusted. When Emperor Xiaowen died and his spirit tablet was enshrined in the ancestral temple, Attendant-in-Ordinary Cui Guang was concurrently serving as Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices. Since the designation of High Ancestor had changed, he reordered the zhao-mu positions accordingly. Inspector-in-Chief of the Censorate and Yellow Gate Attendant Xing Luan argued that even though the High Ancestor had been changed, the zhao-mu order should not be altered. He drafted an impeachment memorial and prepared to bring charges against Cui Guang. Cui Guang said to Huiwei, "This is a matter of ritual, yet the law officers wish to impeach me. I hope I can rely on your help as a leading scholar." Huiwei said, "Your position accords deeply with the principle of adapting ritual to changed circumstances." He soon composed a letter for Guang, explaining and endorsing his position. Cui Guang submitted Huiwei's letter to the chief ministers. Huiwei and Xing Luan were then summoned to debate the matter in court. Minister of the Secretariat Wang Su again sided with Luan, but Luan's argument ultimately failed and the impeachment was dropped.
37
世宗即位之後，仍在左右敷訓經典，自冗從僕射遷祕書丞、武邑郡中正。 惠蔚既入東觀，見典籍未周，乃上疏曰：「臣聞聖皇之御世也，必幽贊人經，參天二地，憲章典故，述遵鴻猷。 故易曰：『觀乎天文以察時變，觀乎人文以化成天下。 』然則六經、百氏，圖書祕籍，乃承天之正術，治人之貞範。 是以溫柔疏遠，詩書之教； 恭儉易良，禮樂之道。 爻彖以精微為神，春秋以屬辭為化。 故大訓炳於東序，藝文光於麟閣。 斯實太平之樞宗，勝殘之要道，有國之靈基，帝王之盛業。 安上靖民，敦風美俗，其在茲乎？ 及秦棄學術，禮經泯絕。 漢興求訪，典文載舉，先王遺訓，燦然復存。 暨光武撥亂，日不暇給，而入洛之書二千餘兩。 魏晉之世，尤重典墳，收亡集逸，九流咸備。 觀其鳩閱史篇，訪購經論，紙竹所載，略盡無遺。 臣學闕通儒，思不及遠，徒循章句，片義無立。 而慈造曲覃，厠班祕省，忝官承乏，唯書是司。 而觀、閣舊典，先無定目，新故雜糅，首尾不全。 有者累帙數十，無者曠年不寫。 或篇第褫落，始末淪殘； 或文壞字誤，謬爛相屬。 篇目雖多，全定者少。 臣今依前丞臣盧昶所撰甲乙新錄，欲裨殘補闕，損併有無，校練句讀，以為定本，次第均寫，永為常式。 其省先無本者，廣加推尋，搜求令足。 然經記浩博，諸子紛綸，部帙既多，章篇紕繆，當非一二校書，歲月可了。 今求令四門博士及在京儒生四十人，在祕書省專精校考，參定字義。 如蒙聽許，則典文允正，羣書大集。 」詔許之。
After Emperor Xuanwu ascended the throne, Huiwei remained at court to expound the classics. He was promoted from Supernumerary Associate Master of Ceremonies to Secretariat Aide and Rectifier of Wuyi Commandery. Once Huiwei entered the Eastern Pavilion and saw that the collection of classics was incomplete, he submitted a memorial saying, "I have heard that when a sage emperor governs the realm, he must exalt the human classics, harmonize with Heaven and Earth, take ancient precedents as his model, and follow the great design of governance." Thus the Classic of Changes says: 'Observe the patterns of Heaven to discern the changes of the times; observe the patterns of culture to transform and complete all under Heaven.' The Six Classics, the hundred schools, and all books and secret archives are the orthodox arts handed down by Heaven and the true standard for governing the people. From them come gentleness and reserve—the teaching of the Classic of Poetry and the Book of Documents; reverence and frugality, ease and goodness—the Way of ritual and music. In the Classic of Changes, subtle precision is the standard; in the Spring and Autumn Annals, linked wording is the means of transformation. Thus great teachings shine in the Eastern Side-chamber of the palace, and literary works gleam in the Qilin Pavilion. This is truly the foundation of great peace, the essential means of overcoming cruelty, the living foundation of empire, and the supreme achievement of emperors and kings. To secure the throne and pacify the people, to strengthen customs and refine morals—is this not their purpose? When the Qin abandoned learning, the rites classics were all but lost. When the Han dynasty rose, it searched far and wide for texts. Canonical writings were recovered, and the instructions of the former kings blazed forth once more. Even when Emperor Guangwu restored order amid chaos, though his days allowed no respite, more than two thousand cartloads of books were brought into Luoyang. In the Wei and Jin periods learning was especially prized. Lost texts were collected and scattered works gathered in, until all nine intellectual traditions were represented. They assembled and reviewed historical records, sought out and purchased classical treatises—hardly any text recorded on paper or bamboo was left uncollected. My own learning falls short of true mastery, and my thought does not reach far. I merely follow chapter and phrase and have achieved nothing of substance. Yet by your gracious favor I have been admitted to the Secretariat. I hold this office only to fill a vacancy, and my sole charge is the books. Yet the old classics housed in the Pavilion and Library have no fixed catalog. New and old texts are jumbled together, and many works are incomplete from beginning to end. Some exist in dozens of bundled fascicles; others have gone years without being copied. Some have lost sections and sequence, with beginnings and endings in ruins; others have damaged text and mistaken characters, errors and corruption piled one upon another. Though the catalog is long, complete and settled copies are few. I now propose to follow the new A-B catalog compiled by my predecessor, Secretariat Aide Lu Chang: to repair damaged passages, fill lacunae, consolidate duplicate and missing texts, collate punctuation, establish a definitive edition, copy it in proper order, and fix it as the permanent standard. For texts the Secretariat currently lacks, I would search widely until complete copies are obtained. Yet the classics are vast and the various masters numerous; with so many fascicles and so much confusion among chapters, this cannot be finished by one or two collators in a matter of months. I therefore request that forty Four Gates Doctors and Confucian scholars resident in the capital be assigned to the Secretariat to specialize in collation and jointly establish the correct readings. If Your Majesty grants this request, the canonical texts will be properly corrected and the entire collection will be brought to order. An edict approved the proposal.
38
又兼黃門侍郎，遷中散大夫，仍兼黃門。 久之，正黃門侍郎，代崔光為著作郎，才非文史，無所撰著，唯自披其傳注數行而已。 遷國子祭酒、祕書監，仍知史事。 延昌二年，追賞侍講之勞，封棗強縣開國男，食邑二百戶。 肅宗初，出為平東將軍、濟州刺史。 還京，除光祿大夫。 魏初已來，儒生寒宦，惠蔚最為顯達。 先單名蔚，正始中，侍講禁內，夜論佛經，有愜帝旨，詔使加「惠」，號惠蔚法師焉。 神龜元年卒于官，時年六十七。 賜帛五百匹，贈大將軍、[5]瀛州刺史，諡曰戴。
He was additionally appointed Yellow Gate Attendant and promoted to Palace Regular Grandee, while retaining his post as Yellow Gate Attendant. After some time he was made regular Yellow Gate Attendant and replaced Cui Guang as Director of Compilation. He lacked talent for history and literature and produced no original work—he merely read through a few lines of his own commentaries. He was transferred to Chancellor of the National University and Director of the Secretariat Library, while continuing to oversee historiographical affairs. In the second year of Yanbei his past service as court reader was rewarded: he was enfeoffed as Founding Baron of Zaoqiang County with a fief of two hundred households. At the beginning of Emperor Xiaoming's reign, he was sent out as General Who Pacifies the East and Governor of Jizhou. On returning to the capital he was appointed Grand Master for Splendid Happiness. From the early Wei period onward, among Confucian scholars from modest backgrounds, none rose so high as Huiwei. He had originally borne the single name Wei. During the Zhengshi era, while lecturing within the inner palace, he discussed Buddhist sutras at night in a manner that pleased the emperor, who ordered the character "Hui" added to his name. He was thereafter known as Master Huiwei. He died in office in the first year of Shenshen, at the age of sixty-seven. Five hundred bolts of silk were bestowed upon his death. He was posthumously granted the title General-in-Chief and Governor of Yingzhou, [5] with the posthumous name Dai.
39
子伯禮，襲封。 伯禮善隸書。 拜奉朝請、員外散騎侍郎、寧朔將軍、步兵校尉、國子博士。 卒，贈輔國將軍、巴州刺史。
His son Bolí inherited the enfeoffment. Bolí was skilled in clerical script. He was appointed Palace Attendant, Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, General Who Pacifies the North, Commandant of Footsoldiers, and Doctor of the National University. At his death he was posthumously granted the title General Who Assists the State and Governor of Bazhou.
40
子產同，襲。 少有才學，早亡，時人惜之。
His son Chantong inherited the title. He showed talent and learning in youth but died young, to the regret of his contemporaries.
41
徐遵明，字子判，華陰人也。 身長八尺，幼孤好學。 年十七，隨鄉人毛靈和等詣山東求學。 至上黨，乃師屯留王聰，受毛詩、尚書、禮記。 一年，便辭聰詣燕趙，師事張吾貴。 吾貴門徒甚盛，遵明伏膺數月，乃私謂其友人曰：「張生名高而義無檢格，凡所講說，不愜吾心，請更從師。 」遂與平原田猛略就范陽孫買德受業。 一年，復欲去之。 猛略謂遵明曰：「君年少從師，每不終業，千里負帙，何去就之甚。 如此用意，終恐無成。 」遵明曰：「吾今始知真師所在。 」猛略曰：「何在？ 」遵明乃指心曰：「正在於此。 」乃詣平原唐遷，納之，居於蠶舍。 讀孝經、論語、毛詩、尚書、三禮，不出門院，凡經六年，時彈箏吹笛以自娛慰。 又知陽平館陶趙世業家有服氏春秋，是晉世永嘉舊本，遵明乃往讀之。 復經數載，因手撰春秋義章，為三十卷。
Xu Zunming, courtesy name Zipan, was a native of Huayin. He stood eight feet tall. Orphaned in youth, he devoted himself to learning. At seventeen he set out with fellow townsman Mao Linghe and others for Shandong to pursue his studies. Reaching Shangdang, he studied under Wang Cong of Tunliu, learning the Mao Commentary on the Odes, the Book of Documents, and the Record of Rites. After a year he left Wang Cong and traveled to Yan and Zhao to study under Zhang Wugui. Zhang Wugui's disciples were very numerous. Zunming studied under him for several months, then confided to a friend, "Master Zhang enjoys great renown but lacks proper restraint. None of his lectures satisfies me—I mean to find another teacher." He then went with Tian Menglue of Pingyuan to study under Sun Maide of Fanyang. After another year, he wished to leave again. Menglue said to him, "You are still young, yet every time you study with a teacher you fail to finish. You carry your texts a thousand li—why are you so restless in coming and going?" With such restlessness, I fear you will never accomplish anything." Zunming replied, "I have now discovered where the true teacher is." Menglue asked, "Where is that?" Zunming pointed to his heart and said, "Right here." He then went to Tang Qian of Pingyuan, who took him in. He lived in a silkworm-rearing shed. He studied the Classic of Filial Piety, the Analects, the Mao Commentary on the Odes, the Book of Documents, and the Three Rites without leaving his courtyard. Six years passed in this way. At times he played the zither and flute to amuse himself. Learning that Zhao Shiye's household in Guantao, Yangping, possessed Fu's Spring and Autumn Annals—an edition dating from the Yongjia era of the Jin—Zunming went there to study it. After several more years he composed his own Explications of the Spring and Autumn Annals in thirty fascicles.
42
是後教授，門徒蓋寡，久之乃盛。 遵明每臨講坐，必持經執疏，然後敷陳，其學徒至今浸以成俗。 遵明講學於外二十餘年，海內莫不宗仰。 頗好聚歛，有損儒者之風。
When he began to teach, his disciples were few; only after a long time did their numbers grow. Whenever Zunming lectured he always held the classic in one hand and the commentary in the other before expounding—a practice his disciples have gradually turned into custom. Zunming taught abroad for more than twenty years, and scholars throughout the realm revered him. He was rather fond of amassing wealth, which somewhat tarnished his reputation as a Confucian scholar.
43
後廣平王懷聞而徵焉。 至而尋退，不好京輦。 孝昌末，南渡河，客於任城。 以兗州有舊，因徙居焉。 永安初，東道大使元羅表薦之，竟無禮辟。 二年，元顥入洛，任城太守李湛將舉義兵，遵明同其事。 夜至民間，為亂兵所害，時年五十五。
Later Prince Huai of Guangping heard of him and summoned him. He arrived but soon withdrew, having no taste for life near the capital. At the end of the Xiaochong era he crossed the Yellow River to the south and took lodging at Rencheng. Because he had old ties in Yan Province, he moved there to settle. At the beginning of Yong'an, Eastern Route Commissioner Yuan Luo recommended him by memorial, but no official summons ever came. In the second year Yuan Hao entered Luoyang. Rencheng Prefect Li Zhan was preparing to raise a loyalist force, and Zunming joined the effort. That night, while among the common people, he was killed by marauding soldiers. He was fifty-five.
44
永熙二年，遵明弟子通直散騎常侍李業興表曰：「臣聞行道樹德，非求利於當年； 服義履仁，豈邀恩於沒世。 但天爵所存，果致式閭之禮； 民望攸屬，終有祠墓之榮。 伏見故處士兗州徐遵明生在衡泌，弗因世族之基； 長於原野，匪乘雕鏤之地。 而託心淵曠，置情恬雅，處靜無悶，居約不憂。 故能垂簾自精，下帷獨得，鑽經緯之微言，研聖賢之妙旨。 莫不入其門戶，踐其堂奧，信以稱大儒於海內，擅明師於日下矣。 是故眇眇四方，知音之類，延首慕德，跂踵依風。 每精廬暫闢，杖策不遠千里； 束脩受業，編錄將踰萬人。 固已企盛烈於西河，擬高蹤於北海。 若慕奇好士，愛客尊賢，罷吏遊梁，紛而成列。 遵明以碩德重名，首蒙禮命，曳裾雅步，眷同置醴。 黃門李郁具所知明，方申薦奏之恩，處心守壑之志，潛居樂道，遂往不歸。 故北海王入洛之初，率土風靡，遵明確然守志，忠潔不渝，遂與太守李湛將誅叛逆。 時有邂逅，受斃凶險。 至誠高節，堙沒無聞，朝野人士，相與嗟悼。 伏惟陛下遠應龍序，俯執天衷，每端聽而忘昃，常坐思而候曉。 雖微功小善，片言一行，莫不衣裳加室，玉帛在門。 況遵明冠蓋一時，師表當世，溘焉冥沒，旌紀寂寥。 逝者長辭，無論榮價，文明敍物，敦厲斯在。 臣託跡諸生，親承顧眄，惟伏膺之義，感在三之重，是以越分陳愚，上諠幄座。 特乞加以顯諡，追以好爵，仰申朝廷尚德之風，下示學徒稽古之利。 若宸鑒昭回，曲垂矜採，則荒墳千載，式貴生平。 」卒無贈諡。
In the second year of Yongxi, Zunming's disciple Direct-and-Regular Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Li Yexing submitted a memorial saying, "I have heard that practicing the Way and cultivating virtue is not done for profit in one's own lifetime;" embracing righteousness and practicing benevolence is not done to seek favor after death." Yet when Heaven's rank endures in a man, the rite of honoring his lane is indeed bestowed; when the people's hopes rest upon him, he ultimately receives the honor of temple and tomb. I humbly observe that the late recluse Xu Zunming of Yan Province was born beside the Heng and Bi streams and owed nothing to a great clan; he grew up in open country, not on inlaid and carved floors. Yet he set his heart on depths and vast spaces, kept his spirit tranquil and refined, lived in quiet without vexation, and in poverty without distress. Thus he could study behind drawn curtains in solitary refinement, penetrating the subtle words of the classics and mastering the profound intent of sages and worthies. Countless scholars entered his gate and reached the inner sanctum of his teaching. Truly he could be called the greatest Confucian of the realm and the preeminent master of his age. From every corner of the realm, those who understood his worth craned their necks in admiration and hastened to follow his example. Whenever he opened his humble school, disciples would travel a thousand li without hesitation; bearing gifts of initiation to receive instruction—those enrolled in his records approached ten thousand. His achievements already rivaled those of the great schools of Xihe, and his stature approached that of the masters of Beihai. Like those who admire the extraordinary, love scholars, honor guests, and revere the worthy—dismissed officials flocking to join the great patrons—they gathered in ranks. Zunming, by his great virtue and eminent reputation, was first to receive a formal summons. He was welcomed with honor, as though fine wine had been placed before a guest of distinction. Yellow Gate Attendant Li Yu understood him well and was about to extend the grace of recommendation when Zunming, resolved to keep to his secluded life, chose quiet study and the Way over office—and departed never to return. When the Prince of Beihai first entered Luoyang and the whole land was swept up in the revolt, Zunming steadfastly held to his principles, loyal and incorruptible. He joined Prefect Li Zhan in planning to suppress the rebellion. By cruel chance he encountered marauding soldiers and met a violent death. Such sincerity and lofty integrity, yet buried in obscurity without public recognition—men of court and countryside alike mourned him. Your Majesty responds to Heaven's mandate from afar and holds the true intent of governance. You listen with full attention past sunset and sit in contemplation awaiting the dawn. Even the slightest merit or smallest good deed, a single word or act—none goes unrewarded with honors at your door. And Xu Zunming had stood at the head of his generation, a teacher and exemplar for the age—yet he was suddenly gone, leaving his honors and memorials all but forgotten. The dead are gone forever; rank and glory aside, what matters is to civilize the world and put things in order—to inspire earnest striving is the point. I myself studied under him and received his personal attention. Bound by reverence and deeply moved by the threefold debt of kindness, I overstep my station to offer this humble plea and lay it before Your Majesty's throne. I beg that he be granted a distinguished posthumous title and noble rank in recognition—upholding the court's esteem for virtue above and showing students below the rewards of classical learning. If Your Majesty's sage judgment looks favorably upon this and shows compassionate acceptance, then even a neglected grave a thousand years hence will stand as lasting honor to his life. In the end no posthumous honors or title were granted.
45
董徵，字文發，頓丘衞國人也。 祖英，高平太守。 父虬，郡功曹。 徵身長七尺二寸，好古，學尚雅素。 年十七，師清河監伯陽，受論語、毛詩、春秋、周易，就河內高望崇受周官，後於博陵劉獻之遍受諸經。 數年之中，大義精練，講授生徒。 太和末，為四門小學博士。 後世宗詔徵入琁華宮，令孫惠蔚問以六經，仍詔徵教授京兆、清河、廣平、汝南四王，後特除員外散騎侍郎。 清河王懌之為司空、司徒，引徵為長流參軍。 懌遷太尉，徵為倉曹參軍。 出為沛郡太守，加揚烈將軍。 入為太尉司馬，俄加輔國將軍。 未幾，以本將軍除安州刺史。 徵因述職，路次過家，置酒高會，大享邑老，乃言曰：「腰龜返國，昔人稱榮； 仗節還家，云胡不樂。 」因誡二三子弟曰：「此之富貴，匪自天降，乃勤學所致耳。 」時人榮之。 入為司農少卿、光祿大夫。 徵出州入卿，匪唯學業所致，亦由汝南王悅以其師資之義，為之啟請焉。 永安初，加平東將軍，尋以老解職。 永熙二年卒。 出帝以徵昔授父業，故優贈散騎常侍、都督相殷滄三州諸軍事、車騎大將軍、儀同三司、尚書左僕射、相州刺史，諡曰文烈。
Dong Zheng, courtesy name Wenfa, was a native of Dunqiu in Weiguo. His grandfather Ying served as Administrator of Gaoping. His father Qiu was Merit Officer of the commandery. Zheng stood seven chi two cun tall. He loved antiquity and pursued learning in a spirit of refined simplicity. At seventeen he studied under Jian Boyang of Qinghe, learning the Analects, Mao's Odes, the Spring and Autumn Annals, and the Book of Changes. He then went to Gao Wangchong of Henei for the Rites of Zhou, and later studied the full canon under Liu Xianzhi of Boling. Within a few years he had mastered the great principles of the classics and began lecturing to students. At the end of the Taihe era he was appointed Erudite of the Four Gates Primary School. Later Emperor Xuanwu summoned Zheng to the Xuanhua Palace and had Sun Huiwei examine him on the Six Classics. He also ordered Zheng to instruct the four princes of Jingzhao, Qinghe, Guangping, and Runan, and later specially appointed him Supernumerary Gentleman of the Palace Cadet. When the Prince of Qinghe, Yi, served as Minister of Works and then Minister over the Masses, he recruited Zheng as Senior Adjutant of the Flowing Staff. When Yi was promoted to Grand Commandant, Zheng became Adjutant of the Granary Bureau. He was sent out as Administrator of Pei Commandery with the additional title General Who Displays Majesty. He returned to the capital as Major of the Grand Commandant and was soon given the additional title General Who Assists the State. Before long he was appointed Inspector of Anzhou, retaining his general's rank. On his way to take up his post, Zheng passed through his home district. He held a grand feast for the local elders and said, "To return to one's homeland wearing the turtle insignia of high office—men of old counted that glory; to return home bearing the imperial staff—why should one not rejoice?" He then admonished his younger relatives: "This wealth and rank did not fall from Heaven—they came from diligent study alone." People of the time admired him for it. He returned to court as Vice Director of the Court of the National Granaries and Grand Master of Splendid Happiness. Zheng's rise from provincial office to court minister owed not only to his scholarship—the Prince of Runan, Yue, also petitioned on his behalf out of respect for their bond as teacher and pupil. At the beginning of the Yong'an era he was given the additional title General Who Pacifies the East, and soon resigned on account of age. He died in the second year of Yongxi. Because Zheng had once been his father's teacher, Emperor Xiaojing generously posthumously honored him as Palace Attendant, Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in Xiang, Yin, and Cang provinces, General of Chariots and Cavalry, Equal in Honor to the Three Ducal Ministers, Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, and Inspector of Xiangzhou, with the posthumous title Wenlie.
46
子仲曜，武定末，儀同開府屬。
His son Zhongyao served at the end of the Wuding era as an aide in a ducal-level office.
47
刁沖，字文朗，勃海饒安人也，鎮東將軍雍之曾孫。 十三而孤，孝慕過人。 其祖母司空高允女，聰明婦人也，哀其早孤，撫養尤篤。 沖免喪後便志學他方，高氏泣涕留之，沖終不止。 雖家世貴達，乃從師於外，自同諸生。 於時學制，諸生悉日直監厨，沖雖有僕隸，不令代己，身自炊爨。 每師受之際，發情精專，不捨晝夜，殆忘寒暑。 學通諸經，偏修鄭說，陰陽、圖緯、算數、天文、風氣之書莫不關綜，當世服其精博。 刺史郭祚聞其盛名，訪以疑義，沖應機解辯，無不祛其久惑。 後太守范陽盧尚之、刺史河東裴植並徵沖為功曹、[6]主簿，非所好也，受署而已，不關事務。 惟以講學為心，四方學徒就其受業者歲有數百。
Diao Chong, courtesy name Wenlang, was a native of Rao'an in Bohai and the great-grandson of General Who Guards the East Yong. Orphaned at thirteen, his filial devotion and grief exceeded that of ordinary men. His grandmother was a daughter of Minister of Works Gao Yun—a wise woman who pitied his early orphanhood and raised him with exceptional devotion. When Chong's mourning period ended he resolved to study elsewhere. The Gaos wept and begged him to stay, but he would not be turned aside. Though his family had been noble and eminent for generations, he went abroad to study under teachers and lived no differently from the other students. Under the school rules of the time, every student took daily turns supervising the kitchen. Though Chong had servants, he would not let them stand in for him and cooked for himself. Whenever he studied under his teachers he gave himself wholly to the work, never resting day or night, scarcely noticing cold or heat. He mastered the full canon, specializing in the Zheng Xuan school, and ranged across works on yin and yang, prognostic lore, mathematics, astronomy, and wind and qi. Contemporaries admired his depth and breadth. Inspector Guo Zuo heard of his fame and consulted him on difficult points. Chong answered on the spot, always clearing away doubts that had long persisted. Later Prefect Lu Shangzhi of Fanyang and Inspector Pei Zhi of Hedong both summoned Chong to serve as Merit Officer [6] and Chief Clerk—posts he did not care for. He accepted the titles in name only and took no part in administrative affairs. Teaching was his sole concern. Each year several hundred students came from all directions to study under him.
48
沖雖儒生，而執心壯烈，不畏強禦。 延昌中，世宗舅司徒高肇擅恣威權，沖乃抗表極言其事，辭旨懇直，文義忠憤。 太傅、清河王懌覽而歎息。
Though a Confucian scholar, Chong had a bold and resolute heart and did not fear the powerful. During the Yanchang era, Emperor Xuanwu's maternal uncle Gao Zhao, Minister over the Masses, wielded power with arrogant impunity. Chong submitted a memorial speaking out boldly—the language earnest and direct, the tone loyal and indignant. Grand Tutor, the Prince of Qinghe Yi, read it and sighed in admiration.
49
先是沖曾祖雍作行孝論以誡子孫，稱：「古之葬者衣之以薪，不封不樹，後世聖人易之棺椁。 其有生則不能致養，死則厚葬過度。 及於末世，至蘧蒢裹尸，倮而葬者。 確而為論，並非折衷。 既知二者之失豈宜同之。 當令所存者棺厚不過三寸，高不過三尺，弗用繒綵，斂以時服。 轜車止用白布為幔，不加畫飾，名為清素車。 又去挽歌、方相，并盟器雜物。 」及沖祖遵將卒，敕其子孫令奉雍遺旨。 河南尹丞張普惠謂為太儉，貽書於沖叔整議其進退。 整令與通學議之，沖乃致書國學諸儒以論其事，學官竟不能答。
Earlier, Chong's great-grandfather Yong had written an Essay on Filial Conduct in Burial to instruct his descendants, saying, "The ancients clothed the dead in firewood for burial, neither raising mounds nor planting trees; later sages replaced this with coffins and outer cases. Yet while their parents lived they failed to provide proper care, and in death they buried them with excessive extravagance. By the decadent age some went so far as to wrap corpses in coarse grass mats and bury them naked. To take either extreme as doctrine is not true moderation. Knowing the failings of both, how can one follow either to the same degree? What should remain is this: coffins no more than three cun thick and three chi high; no colored silks; the dead should be dressed in their ordinary clothes. The funeral carriage should use only a white cloth canopy, with no painted decoration—a carriage called the Plain and Simple Hearse. Also remove dirges, exorcism-mask figures, grave goods, and other such objects. When Chong's grandfather Zun was near death, he charged his descendants to follow Yong's last instructions. Assistant to the Intendant of Henan Zhang Puhui considered the rites too austere and wrote to Chong's uncle Zheng to debate whether to follow them. Zheng had fellow students discuss the matter. Chong then wrote to the Confucian scholars of the Imperial Academy to argue the case, and the academy officials could not answer him.
50
沖以嫡傳祖爵東安侯。 京兆王繼為司空也，並以高選頻辟記室參軍。 肅宗將親釋奠，於是國子助教韓神固與諸儒詣國子祭酒崔光、吏部尚書甄琛，舉其才學，奏而徵焉。 及卒，國子博士高涼及范陽盧道侃、[7]盧景裕等復上狀陳沖業行，議奏諡曰安憲先生，祭以太牢。 子欽，字志儒。 早亡。
As legitimate heir, Chong inherited his grandfather's title, Marquis of Dong'an. When the Prince of Jingzhao Ji served as Minister of Works, he repeatedly recruited Chong for his outstanding talent as Recorder of the Headquarters. When Emperor Xiaoming was about to perform the Confucian vegetable-offering ceremony in person, Imperial University Assistant Erudite Han Sheng and other scholars went to Chancellor Cui Guang of the Imperial Academy and Minister of Personnel Zhen Chen to recommend Chong's talent and learning. A memorial was submitted and he was summoned. After his death, Imperial University Erudite Gao Liang, Lu Daokan [7] of Fanyang, Lu Jingyu, and others submitted a memorial describing Chong's achievements and conduct. The court deliberated and granted him the posthumous title Master Anxian, with sacrifice of the highest grade. His son Qin, courtesy name Zhiru. He died young.
51
盧景裕，字仲儒，小字白頭，范陽涿人也。 章武伯同之兄子。 少聰敏，專經為學。 居拒馬河，將一老婢作食，妻子不自隨從。 又避地大寧山，不營世事，居無所業，惟在注解。 其叔父同職居顯要，而景裕止於園舍，情均郊野，謙恭守道，貞素自得。 由是世號居士。
Lu Jingyu, courtesy name Zhongru, childhood name Baitou, was a native of Zhuo in Fanyang. He was a nephew of Marquis of Zhangwu Tong. From youth he was clever and quick, dedicating himself to the study of the classics. He lived by the Juma River with only an old maidservant to cook for him; his wife and children did not live with him. He also withdrew to Mount Daning, took no part in worldly affairs, and had no occupation beyond writing commentaries. Though his uncle Tong held an eminent post, Jingyu remained in his garden retreat, as content as a man of the fields—humble, devoted to the Way, and quietly satisfied in plain living. For this reason people called him the Recluse.
52
前廢帝初，除國子博士，參議正聲，甚見親遇，待以不臣之禮。 永熙初，以例解。 天平中，還鄉里，與邢子才、魏季景、魏收、邢昕等同徵赴鄴。 景裕寓託僧寺，講聽不已。 未幾，歸本郡。
At the beginning of the Deposed Emperor's reign he was appointed Erudite of the Imperial University and took part in deliberating the standard musical tones. He was greatly favored and treated with the ceremony reserved for one who need not bow as a subject. At the beginning of Yongxi he was dismissed from office according to precedent. During the Tianping era he returned home and was summoned to Ye together with Xing Zicai, Wei Jijing, Wei Shou, and Xing Xin. Jingyu lodged in a Buddhist monastery and never ceased lecturing and attending discussions. Before long he returned to his home commandery.
53
河間邢摩納與景裕從兄仲禮據鄉作逆，逼其同反，以應元寶炬。 齊獻武王命都督賀拔仁討平之。 聞景裕經明行著，驛馬特徵，既而舍之，使教諸子。 在館十日一歸家，隨以鼎食。 景裕風儀言行，雅見嗟賞。 先是景裕注周易、尚書、孝經、論語、禮記、老子，其毛詩、春秋左氏未訖。 齊文襄王入相，於第開講，招延時儁，令景裕解所注易。 景裕理義精微，吐發閑雅。 時有問難，或相詆訶，大聲厲色，言至不遜，而景裕神彩儼然，風調如一，從容往復，無際可尋。 由是士君子嗟美之。
Xing Mona of Hejian and Jingyu's older cousin Zhongli seized their district in rebellion, forcing others to join them in support of Yuan Baoju. Prince Xianwu of Qi ordered Area Commander Heba Ren to suppress the rebellion. Hearing that Jingyu was distinguished in both learning and conduct, he sent post-horses to summon him specially, then released him and had him instruct his sons. While living at the residence he returned home once every ten days and was provided with lavish meals. Jingyu's bearing, speech, and conduct won high admiration. Jingyu had already completed commentaries on the Book of Changes, Book of Documents, Classic of Filial Piety, Analects, Record of Rites, and Laozi; his commentaries on Mao's Odes and the Zuo Tradition of the Spring and Autumn Annals remained unfinished. When Prince Wenxiang of Qi became chancellor, he held lectures at his residence, invited eminent scholars of the age, and had Jingyu expound his commentary on the Changes. Jingyu's reasoning was subtle and refined, and his delivery calm and elegant. When challengers pressed him, some shouted abuse with harsh voices and insolent words—yet Jingyu remained composed, his tone unchanged, answering at ease with no opening for attack. Scholars and gentlemen admired him greatly for it.
54
初，元顥入洛，[8]以為中書郎。 普泰初，復除國子博士。 進退其間，未曾有得失之色。 性清靜，淡於榮利，弊衣粗食，恬然自安，終日端嚴，如對賓客。 興和中，補齊王開府屬，卒於晉陽，齊獻武王悼惜之。
Earlier, when Yuan Hao entered Luoyang, [8] Jingyu was appointed Palace Secretary. At the beginning of Putai he was again appointed Erudite of the Imperial University. Through all these changes of fortune he never showed pleasure or distress. By nature he was quiet and pure, indifferent to rank and profit. In worn clothes and plain food he was content, maintaining all day a dignified bearing as though receiving guests. During the Xinghe era he was appointed aide in the Prince of Qi's office. He died at Jinyang, and Prince Xianwu of Qi mourned him deeply.
